title: Zašto bosanski?
theme: Orientation — what Bosnian is and who this course is for
reviewerNotes: Published for live preview. Orientation chapter — comparative notes intentional on Day 0 only.
storyBeat: Before Ana lands in Sarajevo, we pause for a clear map: what Bosnian is, where the name comes from, how it relates to neighboring standards, who speaks it, and who these lessons are for.

grammar.title: This course teaches Bosnian — Latin script only
grammar.explanation: From Day 1 you will see and type Bosnian in the Latin alphabet (with letters like č, ć, š, ž, đ). Official Bosnian can also appear in Cyrillic, but this course never teaches or displays Cyrillic. One path, one script, less noise.

grammar.title: Close neighbors, separate standards
grammar.explanation: Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian share a common South Slavic dialect base (Štokavian) and are largely mutually intelligible. They are separate standard languages with their own norms, preferred words, and cultural identities. This course teaches standard Bosnian as used in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After today, we will not add “also in Croatian…” sidebars — we stay in Bosnian.

culture.title: A language with a place and a name
culture.body: Bosnian (bosanski) is a South Slavic language and one of the official languages of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Bosna i Hercegovina / BiH). The name comes from the historic region of Bosnia — people have used forms of this name for the speech of the land for centuries. In the 1990s, after independence, Bosnian was codified as a modern standard (with spelling and grammar guides), alongside Croatian and Serbian as official languages of BiH. Speakers often understand one another across those standards, but names matter: calling the language Bosnian honors the country’s identity and the forms you will hear on the streets of Sarajevo, Mostar, and beyond.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A — What is Bosnian, and where does the name come from?
lessonBlocks.body: Bosnian is the standard language taught and used as bosanski jezik in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Etymology (word origin): bosanski comes from Bosna — the name of the region and the river Bosna — plus a Slavic adjective ending, roughly “of Bosnia.” So the language name is tied to place, not to a single invented brand. Linguistically, standard Bosnian is built on the widespread Štokavian dialect shared with neighboring standards. Historically the area sat at a crossroads of Slavic speech, Ottoman administration, and Austro-Hungarian schooling; that history left everyday Bosnian with many familiar Slavic words plus a rich layer of older loanwords from Turkish, Arabic, and Persian (often called orientalisms) that feel at home in BiH conversation — think café culture, food, and everyday politeness. You do not need the full history to start. You need one clear label: you are learning Bosnian.
tips: Say it aloud once: bosanski jezik — Bosnian language
Remember: the name points to Bosnia (Bosna), the place

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B — Why Bosnian is not “just Croatian or Serbian,” and who speaks it
lessonBlocks.body: People often ask: is Bosnian the same as Croatian or Serbian? Honest short answer: speakers can usually understand each other, because the standards grew from the same dialect family — like closely related national standards of one pluricentric language area. Honest longer answer: they are not the same course, the same classroom label, or the same cultural home. Differences show up in preferred vocabulary, some spelling and sound habits (Bosnian standard uses Ijekavian forms, and often keeps an audible h in words where history put it), script choices in public life, and — most of all — identity. Bosnian is an official language of BiH. It is spoken by Bosniaks and by many other people across Bosnia and Herzegovina; it is also spoken in diaspora communities worldwide. Neighbors may call their own standards Croatian or Serbian; mutual understanding does not erase those names. This book teaches Bosnian forms used in everyday BiH life. From Day 1 we will not train you to compare three columns of vocabulary. We will train you to sound at home saying zdravo in Sarajevo.
tips: After Day 0, stay Bosnian-focused — no comparative sidebars

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson C — Why learn Bosnian, and who these lessons are for
lessonBlocks.body: Why Bosnian? Because you care about this place and these people: travel through BiH, family or partners with roots here, work or study tied to the region, diaspora kids reclaiming a home language, or simple curiosity about a culture that is too often folded into a vague “Balkans” label. Learning Bosnian says you want the local name, the local café talk, and the local story. Who is this course for? Absolute beginners and false beginners who read English. Adults and older teens who can spend about an hour a day. Travelers, partners, students, and self-learners who want Latin-script Bosnian only — clear goals, culture, puzzles, and a silly story with Ana (the learner), Emir (the guide), Amira (the café owner), and Mrvica (the cat). Who it is not trying to be: a linguistics degree, a three-language comparative grammar, or a Cyrillic course. Book 1 moves from first greetings (Day 1) toward early A2 across 30 lessons. Day 0 is your map. Day 1 is your first step onto the stone streets of Baščaršija.

funFacts.title: Etymology in one line
funFacts.body: Bosanski is basically “Bosnian / of Bosnia” — the language name is anchored in the place name Bosna.

funFacts.title: Official, not obscure
funFacts.body: Bosnian is an official language of Bosnia and Herzegovina, used in schools, media, and daily life — not a dialect label invented for tourists.

funFacts.title: Mutual understanding, separate classrooms
funFacts.body: A traveler who learns Bosnian will understand a lot next door — and still be studying a named standard with its own books, news, and pride.

funFacts.title: Why we skip Cyrillic here
funFacts.body: Less split attention. Master Latin Bosnian first; you can explore other scripts later if you want.

The Bosnian language (and adjective) we are learning

questions.question: The name bosanski is etymologically tied to…
questions.explanation: Bosanski comes from Bosna — the region/place name — plus a Slavic adjective ending.

questions.question: How should you think about Bosnian vs Croatian/Serbian for this course?
options: Identical in every word, so labels do not matter
Closely related, largely mutually intelligible standards — we teach Bosnian forms and stay Bosnian-focused after Day 0
We will memorize three parallel columns every day
questions.explanation: They are close and often mutually intelligible, but this course teaches Bosnian and does not become a three-way comparative class.

questions.question: Who speaks Bosnian?
options: People in and from Bosnia and Herzegovina (and diaspora communities), as an official language of BiH
questions.explanation: Bosnian is an official language of BiH and is spoken in the country and in diaspora communities.

questions.question: Which script does Learn Bosnian teach?
options: Both every day from the start
questions.explanation: Latin script only — a deliberate choice to keep the path clear.
